clue.text: Smoker among lots that are typically Scottish

definitions.text: Smoker among lots that are typically Scottish

indicators.note: to be among a crowd is to stand inside it, so the smoker sits within the lots

blocks.note: bags of something = lots of it
a pipe is something you smoke

explanation.surface: A remark about Scottish smokers, as though puffing were a national habit.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: a pipe sitting inside bags is a fair picture of the instrument itself, a bag with drone and chanter pipes stuck into it.
explanation.definitionFit: The instrument is a leather bag fitted with several reed pipes, and it is the emblematic sound of Scotland.

clue.text: Back an attempt

blocks.note: the article kept as it is
a try or turn, as in 'have a bash at it'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads as a verb, to support an attempt, but it is the adverb of time: years back, years before now.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words place an event in the past: 'ten years back' and 'ten years before now' mean the same thing.

clue.text: Proper, before start of party, to preen

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only the first of 'party' is used

explanation.surface: Someone getting properly dressed up before heading off to a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' just places the first piece ahead of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to groom yourself fussily, tidying hair and clothes in front of a mirror.

clue.text: Fresh respect due to the victimised

indicators.note: something made fresh is made anew, so the letters of 'respect due' are remade in a new order

explanation.surface: A plea that victims should be shown new respect.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is used as a collective noun here, 'the persecuted', matching 'the victimised'.
explanation.definitionFit: Those picked on, harassed and ill-treated by others are victims of persecution; the two phrases name the same group.

clue.text: Some weeks of term are quieter

indicators.note: only some of the letters in 'weeks of term' are used, a run that crosses the word breaks

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of weeks into the start of term

explanation.surface: A student noting that part of the school term is calmer than the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer starts with the last letter of 'weeks' and ends inside 'term'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lower in volume: a softer voice or softer music is simply less loud, the same comparative sense.

clue.text: Concisely states problems at university

blocks.note: a student in residence is 'up' at university

explanation.surface: A student at university stating their troubles in a few words.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge is British usage for being in residence as a student; going 'down' is leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a summary is to express the main points briefly, the phrasal verb's everyday sense.

clue.text: Say what Pooh played with in mythical river

indicators.note: to say a word is to speak it, so what counts is the sound of the playthings, not their spelling

blocks.note: Winnie-the-Pooh invented Poohsticks, dropping sticks off a bridge

explanation.surface: A question about Winnie-the-Pooh's game on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: Poohsticks, from A. A. Milne's books, is played by dropping sticks into a river from a bridge, which keeps the river in the surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the dead are ferried by Charon across this river to reach the underworld.

clue.text: Expedient to be just in time for work?

definitions.text: to be just in time for work?

blocks.note: a stopgap, something improvised to serve for now

blocks.clueFragment: to be just in time for work?
blocks.note: read as two words: to arrive in time to make (catch) your shift at work

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether it pays to arrive at work at the last minute.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, whimsical reading: 'make' as in make the train, plus a work shift.
explanation.definitionFit: An expedient is a temporary improvised measure, and a makeshift arrangement is exactly a stopgap.

clue.text: Rival outlet collapsed — it's not to be seen

indicators.note: a collapsed structure lies in pieces, so the letters of 'rival outlet' fall into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A competing shop has gone under and vanished from the high street.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic description: the answer is radiation beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Human eyes cannot detect light of these short wavelengths, so it is invisible radiation.

clue.text: Manager installing one item of office equipment

indicators.note: to install something is to put it inside, so 'manager' takes 'one' within it

explanation.surface: An office manager setting up a new machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manager' wants to be a boss; here it is simply someone who manages, i.e. copes.
explanation.definitionFit: A photocopying machine is standard kit found in almost every workplace alongside printers and phones.

clue.text: Experimentally launch a bird of prey?

definitions.text: Experimentally launch a bird of prey?

blocks.note: surface reading: an idiom for floating an idea to test reactions
setter's reading: the kite is also a hawk-like raptor, so sending one aloft is literal

explanation.surface: A falconer trying out a hawk in flight for the first time.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means to test public opinion with a trial proposal; the question mark admits the bird pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes putting out a tentative suggestion to gauge reaction before committing to it.

clue.text: Liqueur prices let rip

indicators.note: to let something rip is to let it run wild, so the letters of 'prices let' go wild

explanation.surface: A bar letting its drink prices soar out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let rip' looks like one phrase, but 'let' is part of the fodder and 'rip' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a clear orange-flavoured spirit, a sweet after-dinner drink used in cocktails like the margarita.

clue.text: Compensation as preliminary work not begun

indicators.note: something not begun is missing its start, so the phrase for preliminary work loses its opening letter

blocks.note: preparations are the groundwork done beforehand

explanation.surface: Being paid for groundwork on a job that never started.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the first P and the groundwork becomes the payout.
explanation.definitionFit: Payments made to make amends for a wrong, especially by a defeated nation after war, are a form of recompense.

clue.text: Test, for example, taken twice

blocks.note: 'as' introduces an example: cities as London
the second helping of 'for example': say, London

explanation.surface: An exam where each example must be done twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For example' is used twice with two different synonyms, one after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: An assay is an analysis of a metal or substance to find its purity, a chemical trial.

clue.text: Tension so high always in loud playing field

indicators.note: one thing being in another puts 'always' inside 'loud'

blocks.note: f = forte, the musical mark for loud

explanation.surface: The noisy, nervy atmosphere at a big football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loud playing' looks like a musical phrase, but 'playing field' belongs together; a pitch is the British word for a sports field.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a state of extreme excitement or agitation, when feelings run at their peak.

clue.text: Pork unpopular, but stuff oneself

blocks.note: out of favour, as in 'out' of fashion

explanation.surface: A diner who dislikes pork still eating greedily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pork unpopular' reads as a verdict on the meat; it is two separate pieces, the animal and 'out' in the sense of out of favour.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for eating greedily and to excess, gorging on food until full.

clue.text: Prime minister pleased to put on some weight

blocks.note: a stone is a British unit of weight, 14 pounds

explanation.surface: A leader happy to be gaining a few pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To put on' reads as gaining weight, but it just places one piece after the other. A stone (14 lb) is still how Britons give body weight.
explanation.definitionFit: William Gladstone led Victorian Britain's government four times, a Liberal statesman.

clue.text: Stars, say, returning car

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the abbreviation for 'say' is read backwards

blocks.note: the Mini, a classic British small car

explanation.surface: Film stars bringing back a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests celebrities, but it is a constellation of stars.
explanation.definitionFit: The Twins is a zodiac constellation whose brightest points are Castor and Pollux.

clue.text: Academic not quite prepared to meet monarch

indicators.note: not quite complete means falling short at the end, so the word for prepared loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A lecturer nervously getting ready for an audience with the king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To meet' simply joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In British universities this title is a senior teaching rank, just below professor.

clue.text: Learnt about flat charge

indicators.note: turned about means moved around, so the letters of 'learnt' are moved around

explanation.surface: Someone finding out about a fixed fee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat charge' reads as a fixed fee; it is the money charged for renting a flat (apartment).
explanation.definitionFit: The amount paid by a tenant to a landlord for an apartment is its rent.

clue.text: Farewell unduly protracted?

blocks.note: taken literally the two words mean at such great length

explanation.surface: A goodbye that drags on too long.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal second reading of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a casual parting expression, like 'see you' or 'goodbye'.

clue.text: Time to wear scarf from secret store

indicators.note: a body wearing a garment is inside it, so 'time' goes inside 'scarf'

blocks.note: a sash is a band of cloth worn over the shoulder or waist

explanation.surface: Taking a scarf out of a hidden hoard when the cold sets in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time to wear scarf' reads as a weather remark; 'to wear' is the instruction to put one piece inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden hoard, a hoard of things tucked away, is exactly what the noun names.

clue.text: Craftsman worried, having to work with others

blocks.note: ate = worried, as in 'what's eating you?'

explanation.surface: A craftsman anxious about having to join a team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worried' looks like anxious; it is the past tense of 'eat' in the sense of gnaw at.
explanation.definitionFit: To act jointly with colleagues toward a shared goal is the verb's plain meaning.

clue.text: Bar is raised for wild enjoyment

indicators.note: in a down clue raising something lifts it bottom to top, so the word for bar is read upwards

blocks.note: a lever is a bar used to prise things

explanation.surface: A pub raising its bar to make room for a wild party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub; it is a metal bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisy, lively celebration full of merrymaking is a revel.

clue.text: Used teeth to eat a tempting morsel

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so 'used teeth' swallows 'a'

blocks.note: the article kept as it is

explanation.surface: Someone biting into a delicious titbit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used teeth' is a roundabout past tense of bite, and the whole phrase wraps round the little word 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Food placed on a hook or in a trap to lure fish or animals is the lure.

clue.text: A party given to officer and men in state

blocks.note: other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: A party thrown for an officer and his men somewhere in a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given to' places A PARTY after the other pieces. A 'do' is British slang for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the fifty US states, in the Rocky Mountains, capital Denver.

clue.text: Pub returning tax to European sailors

indicators.note: returning is going back, so the tax word is read backwards

blocks.note: value added tax, the British sales tax

explanation.surface: A pub handing a tax refund to visiting European sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' only affects the tax; 'to' then joins the other pieces after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn or alehouse where drinks are served, an older word for a bar.

clue.text: Whiskey, port and bitter called for

indicators.note: 'called' is spoken, so the word for bitter is taken by its sound

explanation.surface: An order at the bar: whiskey, port and a pint of bitter.
explanation.walkthrough: Three routes: rye whiskey, Rye the old port town in Sussex, and the sound of 'wry'. Bitter is also a British beer, which feeds the drinks surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye whiskey is distilled from that grain; Rye in East Sussex is one of the historic Cinque Ports.

clue.text: Appearance of a ghost about to disappear

indicators.note: whatever disappears is gone, so the word for 'about' vanishes from the ghost

blocks.note: the article kept as it is

explanation.surface: A ghostly apparition that is about to vanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to disappear' reads as 'on the point of vanishing'; split it, and 'about' is the part that goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's look or outward features, their mien, is their aspect.

clue.text: For a change, have logs to share

indicators.note: a change rearranges things, so the letters of 'have logs' take a new order

explanation.surface: A suggestion to split firewood for once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a change' reads as 'for once'; here it is the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To split a cost equally with someone, each paying fifty per cent, is to divide it.
